before.approach: Drive Road 38 west from Mosquito Lake Road, cross Clearwater Creek at about 4.5 miles, and take the right fork down to the gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack. From the gate, the approach is entirely on old logging roads and then ridge/brush for roughly 7 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car-to-summit, one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble — most parties mountain-bike the road portion to save time and legs. Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and ascend the well-graded logging road for about 2.5 miles; at the first major fork stay right (the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry). About 0.2 miles later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the left branch here. Around the 5-mile mark, near a dirt mound and a cairn, leave the logging road proper and pick up an old, overgrown road spur that switchbacks up through a clearcut; this is the point where route-finding gets harder and the brush thickens noticeably (expect to get soaked in wet weather — the clearcut brush is notorious for saturating pants and boots even without rain). By about 6.4 miles you pass an old fire-ring in the clearcut and enter a final band of brush before reaching timber at the base of the west ridge; from there, follow the timbered ridge itself up to where it opens onto rock and the class 3 scrambling begins. There is no reliable water source once you leave the river at the trailhead, so carry what you need for the day. In low cloud/fog, which is common on the Twin Sisters, the clearcut and lower-ridge sections lack obvious cairns or a defined tread and route-finding can be genuinely difficult; parties should be comfortable navigating by map/GPS through brushy, featureless clearcut terrain. On the ridge proper, cairns mark a Class 3 line — the key beta repeated across trip reports is to stay LEFT (climber's left) on the crest; drifting right leads toward false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 terrain on loose, exposed rock.

pitch_detail.notes: Climbers' trail and broken talus/boulder slopes from the end of the bike route up to the base of the ridge.
Sustained scrambling on orange-weathered dunite, staying south/left of the crest through the 'Katie Gap' notch (~6,300 ft) that bypasses a cliff band.
Final scramble up blocky terrain to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack bridge gate, the logging roads to the cairn at mile 5, then the clearcut spur to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
This is a Twin Sisters approach, so start with the range check: the Twin Sisters here are the olivine peaks west of Mount Baker, reached off Mosquito Lake Road and the Middle Fork Nooksack. Every road name below belongs to that range and to no other Twin Sisters.

Drive Road 38 west from Mosquito Lake Road, cross Clearwater Creek, and take the right fork down to the gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack. From the gate it is roughly 7 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car to summit, almost all of it on old logging road and then ridge — one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble, and most parties mountain-bike the road.

Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and climb the well-graded logging road about 2.5 miles. At the first major fork stay RIGHT; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the LEFT branch.

Around mile 5 the road walking ends. From there an old overgrown spur switchbacks up through a clearcut, and by about mile 6.4 you pass an old fire ring and enter a final band of brush before timber at the base of the west ridge.

The roads are on private timberland; access status changes, so confirm before the trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the scramble. In May and June parties still get up it but the north-slope snowfield is in play
hazards: Route-finding through a featureless clearcut with no cairns and no tread, in the cloud that is normal here
Brush that saturates clothing and boots without rain
Drifting right on the crest into unintended Class 4-5 on loose, exposed rock
Private timberland access that changes year to year
No water after the river at the gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRT MOUND AND CAIRN AT ABOUT MILE 5 IS THE MOST IMPORTANT MARKER ON THIS APPROACH, BECAUSE IT IS WHERE THE NAVIGATION GETS HARD. Up to there you are on graded logging road and the only decisions are two forks — RIGHT at the first major fork about 2.5 miles in, then LEFT at the next fork 0.2 mile past the second bridge. At the mound and cairn near mile 5, leave the road for an old overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut.

THE FIRE RING AT ABOUT MILE 6.4 IS THE SECOND MARKER, and it confirms you took the right spur. Past it is a final band of brush and then timber at the base of the west ridge.

IN LOW CLOUD, WHICH IS NORMAL HERE, THE CLEARCUT IS THE HARDEST GROUND ON THE ROUTE AND IT IS NOT THE MOUNTAIN. There are no cairns and no defined tread through the clearcut and lower ridge, and the terrain is genuinely featureless. Parties should be prepared to navigate this section by map and GPS. The brush will also soak you to the waist without any rain falling.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: follow the timbered ridge up until it opens onto rock. Trees stop, rock starts, Class 3 begins. There is no bergschrund, no notch and no col to look for — the transition is vegetative.

THE ONE PIECE OF BETA THAT REPEATS IN EVERY ACCOUNT, AND IT IS THE FOG TEST FOR THE RIDGE ITSELF: STAY LEFT — CLIMBER'S LEFT — ON THE CREST. Cairns mark a Class 3 line that way. Drifting RIGHT leads to false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 ground on loose, exposed rock. If the climbing has got harder than Class 3 and the rock has got worse, you have drifted right; traverse back left rather than pushing on.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS A CONFIRMATION YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT RANGE. The Twin Sisters are dunite — olivine-rich ultramafic rock, exceptionally grippy, commonly compared to coarse sandpaper. If the rock under your hands is ordinary Cascade granite or volcanic rubble, you are not on the Sisters.

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate at the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, then the Dailey Prairie roads to the West Ridge path
approach_variants.notes:
The same gate and ridge, described by road names with the Dailey Prairie road-end as the marker: via Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38. Park at the gate near 1,200 ft and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads — commonly by mountain bike — to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.

Several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie make GPS or a GPX track genuinely useful here; wrong turns on this network are common and expensive.

The gate situation on this network changes year to year. Treat the drivable road-end as unverified until confirmed for your trip.
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network around Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
Private-timberland gates whose status changes year to year
The same drift-right-into-Class-5 trap on the ridge crest
Brushy, wet climbers' path with no maintained tread
Long approach with no water above the road network
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROAD NETWORK IS THE CRUX AND THE MOUNTAIN IS NOT. Around Dailey Prairie the logging roads fork repeatedly with no signage, every branch looks like the main line, and a wrong turn costs miles. Carry a track. THE END OF RIDEABLE ROAD IS THE MARKER, and on this network it is commonly identified by a LARGE CULVERT PIPE at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes there and continue on foot. THE CLIMBERS' PATH IS BRUSHY AND WET AND NOT HARD TO FOLLOW — that combination is itself the confirmation. It climbs through timber onto the ridge crest. ARRIVAL: the same as the other variant, because it is the same ridge. Timber gives way to rock and Class 3 scrambling starts. On the crest, STAY CLIMBER'S LEFT; drifting right puts you on false summits and unintended Class 4-5 ground. WHICH SISTER AM I ON? This matters because the same road network serves North Twin, South Twin, Little Sister, Cinderella and Skookum, and the peaks look alike. NORTH TWIN's west ridge tops out at 6,644 ft and is reached from the road network north of the range. SOUTH TWIN's west ridge is gained at an obvious NOTCH in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft above Orsino Creek Basin, and its summit is 7,004 ft. If your ridge started at a defined notch, you are on South Twin.

before.beta: From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead, hike ~4.7 miles through forest and meadows to the PCT, then follow the PCT north/west around the mountain's flank to its high point. Leave the PCT on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus on Old Snowy's south side to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.
before.approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). The first stretch climbs gently through forest for roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old Bypass Trail/Trail 96A (stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line). Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~6,400 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Continue past the Trail 97 junction (west to Cispus Basin/PCT) and the Trail 86 junction (Goat Lake), staying on the main track as it climbs in long benches with Mount Adams and the Goat Rocks opening up behind you. At about 4.7 miles the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 7,100 ft; turn right (north) onto the PCT. Follow the PCT north for about 1.8 miles, traversing rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill terrain below Old Snowy's south ridge - snow patches can linger here into midsummer and may require an ice axe/traction for a secure traverse in early season. Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's south ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble: the last few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers. Total one-way distance is approximately 7.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain; round trip is roughly 15.5 miles, typically taking 8.5-9.5 hours car to car.

climbing_route.label: Final few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit
climbing_route.notes: The last few hundred feet are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the south ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old bypass trail — stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 6,400 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Continue past the two trail junctions to the PCT at roughly 7,100 ft and turn right, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill below Old Snowy's south ridge.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul through Sep, most reliable in August
hazards: An unmarked, easily missed turn off the PCT — the route's one real navigation problem
A persistent snowfield on the PCT traverse below the summit, firm and icy in early morning
Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
High wind and lightning exposure on an open crest, with common afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once off the PCT
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the wilderness
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TURN OFF THE PCT IS UNMARKED, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING ON THIS ROUTE YOU CAN GET WRONG.

THE TEST THAT WORKS IN FOG IS ABOUT MOTION, NOT LANDMARKS: the PCT here is SIDEHILLING — traversing across the slope. The climbers' path is THE FIRST THING THAT TURNS UPHILL AND STOPS CONTOURING, branching right, east, toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's south ridge. Take the first thing that climbs.

THE NEGATIVE IS EQUALLY MECHANICAL: IF THE PCT STARTS DESCENDING ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE TURN. Go back; do not climb straight up from where you noticed.

DISTANCE CROSS-CHECK: about 1.8 miles north of the Trail 96 junction at 7,100 ft, and the path switchbacks steeply for about half a mile from where you leave the trail.

SECOND MARKER, AND IT SITS BEFORE THE TURN RATHER THAN AFTER IT: a persistent SNOWFIELD on the PCT below the summit lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot on the exposed sidehill traverse. Meeting it means the turn is still ahead of you. It is firmest and safest crossed in the morning.

A SOFT CONFIRMATION AT THE SADDLE, WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS VISIBLE FROM A DISTANCE: many parties stash trekking poles there for the scramble. A cache of poles on a rocky saddle is a good sign you are at the right one.

BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE: the last few hundred feet to the summit is Class 2-3 hands-and-feet on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rock knocked down by parties above is the hazard, so do not stack directly below other climbers.

AND A NEGATIVE THAT IS ABOUT VISIBILITY RATHER THAN GROUND: once you leave the PCT there is no maintained tread. Poor visibility is the recorded route-finding difficulty on this peak, and the honest response is to turn round at the PCT rather than to search for the spur.

before.rope_note: Class 2-3 non-technical scramble via PCT/south ridge in the Goat Rocks; well-graded trail to a short loose/exposed final scramble. No rope needed under normal summer conditions.
obj_haz: loose volcanic rockfall on the summit scramble
early/mid-season snow and old glacier ice on the Packwood Glacier PCT crossing
sudden alpine weather and lightning exposure
route-finding on the unsigned summit spur
before.detailed_rack: No rack is needed — this is an unroped scramble. Trekking poles are widely used and typically stashed just below the final scramble; in early season (persistent snow on the PCT alternate and the Packwood Glacier crossing) an ice axe and microspikes/traction devices are commonly carried for self-arrest and secure footing.

pro_tips: Aim for the crest of the southwest ridge rather than grinding straight up the direct talus line — several parties report it's easier on the legs and faster
Camp at Lake Doris/Freds Pass or Dorothy Lake/Shellrock Pass to combine Osceola with Mount Carru and/or Mount Lago on the same trip
Move deliberately and focus on foot placement on the talus — ankle injury from loose rock is the main real risk on this route

before.rappels: None required on the standard south-side descent — the east ridge is normally downclimbed to the col. Parties who take the 5.7 variation on the north side of the summit blocks generally make one or two single-rope rappels off slung blocks to regain the ridge. If you continue north out of the col instead of returning to Crescent Creek Basin (i.e. toward the Mustard Glacier and Picket Pass), budget three or more rappels off improvised anchors — a 2011 party built theirs from a driven piton, a slung block and a nut in a constriction, then rappelled the broken couloir and glacier spilling off the north side.
before.descent_text: Reverse the east ridge — 200-250 ft of blocky Class 3 with a short Class 4 step, downclimbed by most parties. If you climbed the 5.7 variation on the north side of the summit blocks, one or two single-rope rappels off slung blocks put you back on the ridge crest; back the anchor up, because the rock here has proven itself capable of moving. From the Otto-Himmel col descend the snow and glacier slopes south back into Crescent Creek Basin. The critical detail here is the moat and bergschrund where the snow meets the rock: it is a non-event when snow-filled in early season and can become an overhanging pit by August. One party descending the equivalent feature on the north side had to jump a large overhanging moat and then climb out the far side with an ice axe. Scout the crossing on the way up and remember where it was. Do NOT descend north out of the col unless you are deliberately continuing toward the Mustard Glacier and Picket Pass — that side takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors down a broken couloir and glacier. From Crescent Creek Basin, recross the Barrier at about 6,100 ft (the steep grassy ledges are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired), traverse Terror Basin at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, then drop the 5,000 ft climbers' path to the stone arrow at 1,700 ft and follow the old roadbed out to Goodell Creek. Give the descent of the climbers' path real respect — it is steep, loose, brushy and hard on knees, and the exit is where most parties are moving slowest.
